newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican bonds to start domestic trade on Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: Mexican bonds to start domestic trade on Tuesday.

text.p: A number of Mexico's outstanding Brady and federal government bonds will begin trading on the Mexican stock exchange on Tuesday, a step that officials say will create a long-term debt market in Mexico.

"For the first time in the history of the BMV (Mexico's stock market), external debt issued by the government of Mexico will be able to be traded in this country," Gerardo Flores, chief operating officer of the stock exchange, said on Monday.

Speaking at the stock exchange, Deputy Finance Minister Martin Werner said the move will open direct access for local investors to public debt, increase their investment opportunities and create a long-term debt market in Mexico.
The dollar-denominated instruments will be settled in pesos.
Mexico roared back to capital markets following the peso crash of late 1994, placing about $15 billion worth of debt in external markets in 1996.
The titles that will be listed include some of that debt issued as Mexico rebuilt its yield curve. The federal government issues its debt under the name the United Mexican States (UMS).
The Finance Ministry said that the first debt instruments to be listed will be the:
-UMS 01, 9.75 percent.
-UMS 01, FRN Libor +2.
-UMS 07, 9.875 percent.
-UMS 16, 11.375 percent.
-UMS 26, 11.50 percent.
-UMS 19, Par 6.25 percent.
-UMS 19, Discount Libor + 0.8125 percent.
"The reason we picked the issues that we did is that they conformed to Mexico's yield curve," Werner said.
He said the issues were also extremely liquid.
Werner said the total amount of those seven debt issues is about $30 billion, but he predicted the part that will be traded within Mexico will grow gradually.
In the medium-term, between 10 and 20 percent of that outstanding listed debt could eventually trade in Mexico.
He added the govenment could issue more debt to maintain a representative yield curve.
Officials said the move was a step in the Mexican stock market's move toward becoming a more international market.

The instruments will be traded by brokerage houses and banks and the government believes the buyers will be financial institutions, public investors, institutional investors, investment funds and the new government pension funds.
Analysts said that in its initial operations the titles will likely not be heavily traded.

"The domestic demand for the international debt instruments will be relatively small, due to the fact that the large banks can fill their demand for these types of instruments in the exterior," said ING Baring's director of analysis in Mexico, Sergio Martin.
